BREAKING: The number of restaurants in New York dropped ~2,000 YoY in Q1 2026, posting its largest YoY decline in at least 36 years.

This surpasses even the worst contraction recorded in any quarter during the 2020 pandemic.

The number of eating and drinking places in New York State has now declined YoY for 4 consecutive quarters, its longest streak since 2021.

This comes as restaurants are facing surging operating expenses, including insurance premiums, wages, interest rates, utilities, and health coverage, with overall costs rising faster than national averages.

Last year, employee health insurance costs jumped +12.9% for New York-area service firms, business insurance rose +7.0%, while utility costs surged +8.5%, according to the Manhattan Chamber of Commerce.

Skyrocketing costs are crushing New York restaurants.

"Most people are afraid to be wrong." - Howard Marks on why nobody gets out in time.

The market goes up most years, so the only way to look wrong is to be out of it. 

But nobody wants to look wrong, so nobody gets out. Until a crisis does it for them, at the bottom.

Marks got out in 2006, looked wrong for a year and a half, and had $11 billion ready when 2008 hit.

There is now $270 billion chasing a yield that keeps blowing up.

Derivative-income ETFs have exploded from barely $1 billion in 2020 to about $270 billion in 2026, more than doubling since 2024, as investors hunt for passive income. The problem is the product itself: you collect a rich distribution while the underlying price gets hammered.

Younger investors should own growth. Reaching for conservative income while risk-free Treasuries pay 5% is taking equity risk for no reason.

Refiners are printing money while drivers get squeezed.

The 321 crack spread, the margin for turning crude into gasoline and diesel, hit a record this quarter, topping the 2020 and 2022 peaks near $60 a barrel. When fuel-making margins blow out like this, the refiners capture the spread and every driver pays the other side.

An energy price shock always has a winner. Right now it is the refiner, not the pump.

$VLO

tweets.text:
The US just crossed a line it has never crossed in peacetime.

Federal interest costs hit a record $1 trillion. Debt held by the public is heading past 115% of GDP, set to break the 1946 wartime record by 2030, and net interest eats a record share of GDP. Higher debt plus higher rates is a snowball: interest forces more borrowing, which lifts rates, which lifts interest.

There is one politically easy exit, and it runs through the printing press. That is the real tail risk for the dollar.

The US is running a wartime-size deficit in a full-employment economy.

The 2026 budget gap hit $1.99 trillion, more than 6% of GDP, with unemployment still low. Deficits this large normally only appear in a recession or a war. Running one now means the fiscal cushion is already spent before the next downturn arrives.

When the slowdown comes, the gap explodes from here. That is how a debt problem becomes a currency problem.

tweets.text:
Brazil's economy is still growing, barely.

The central bank's GDP-proxy index rose 0.34% in August and 1.21% from a year ago, a mild expansion well below the pace of a few years back. High rates are doing their job, cooling a once-hot economy toward stall speed.

This is the soft landing every other central bank is chasing: growth that slows without snapping. The open question is whether it holds from here.

The stock everyone calls the AI bubble is now priced like a value stock.

Nvidia trades at about 13 times forward earnings, its cheapest multiple in years. The price kept climbing, but estimated earnings climbed faster, so the valuation compressed. The most argued-over stock on the planet is cheaper on its numbers than it has been in a decade.

Either those earnings hold and it is a bargain, or they roll over and the low multiple was a trap. That is the whole AI debate in one number.

$NVDA
